summary: This unit teaches you to plan a complete fabrication job, from the first enquiry to the final review, as a Level 3 welder or team leader. You will learn to pin down the scope and objectives, gather and check the information, break the job into tasks, build a bar chart with the critical path and float, plan people, equipment and materials, estimate time and cost, plan for safety, permits, quality and the unexpected, present the plan for approval, track progress and changes, and close out and review the job.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). At Level 2 you plan your own task. At Level 3 you plan a **complete activity** for a team: a set of grilles for a school, a canopy for a clinic, a repair during a factory shutdown. You decide what will be done, in what order, by whom, with what, for how much and by when, and how you will know it was done right.

A good plan saves money, keeps people safe and keeps promises to clients. A poor plan shows up as steel ordered too late, two jobs fighting over one welding machine, a frame painted before anyone checked its welds, and a client told the wrong date.
**Who it is for:** Welding Level 3 trainees at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres, and welders who lead jobs or teams.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means on a fabrication job
rows: Agree the scope (what is and is not included), clear objectives and the finish date; gather and check the drawings, specification, standards and WPS; visit the site.
Break down and sequence the work
Split the job into tasks, put them in a sensible order, and show which tasks must wait for others.
Draw a bar chart, find the critical path, the float and the milestones, and set a baseline.
Work out the people and skills, machines and materials each task needs, and when; make the cut list and the order list, allowing for lead times.
Add up labour, materials, outside work, equipment and consumables; add a contingency; show GCT at the current rate.
Plan for safety and the unexpected
Assess the risks, name the permits (hot work, confined space, lifting, height), set the emergency arrangements and the backup plans.
Write an inspection and test plan with hold points, acceptance criteria and records.
Present the plan to the supervisor, the client and the team, each with the information they need.
Track progress, deal with delays, breakdowns and changes, and keep a daily record.
Final inspection, snag list, handover, as-built records, filing, and a review that makes the next plan better.

ul: A **multiple-choice paper** on scope, scheduling, resources, estimating, risk and permits, quality planning, monitoring, changes and close-out. Several questions need a short calculation (days, float, lengths of stock, costs, percentages).

A **written paper**: short answers with exact terms (Gantt chart, lead time, baseline, snag list, as-built drawing, request for information, first-off) and sums; and longer answers in full sentences, for example finding the critical path of a job, or planning a hot-work job in a working building.

**Practical tasks** done as a team: prepare and present a complete plan for a fabrication contract; and plan, make and review a small fabrication job (such as two steel trestles), keeping to a hold point and tracking progress on a wall chart.

blocks.note: Show your working on every schedule and estimate. A marker, a supervisor or a client must be able to follow how you reached each date and each figure, and an error is easy to find when every step is written down.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Defining the job: scope, objectives and information

blocks.p: Planning starts before the first task: you must know exactly what the job is. Most overruns and arguments start with a scope that nobody pinned down.
The **scope** says what will be done and what will not. The things left out are called **exclusions**. Write both down, because the client will assume that anything not excluded is included.

head: In scope (example: a steel canopy over a clinic entrance)
Not in scope, unless agreed
rows: Make and fit a canopy frame about 6 m × 3 m to the drawing, at its latest revision
Supply and fix the roof sheeting and gutter
Prime and paint two coats in the colour agreed
Concrete bases for the posts (by the client's builder)
Lighting under the canopy (by an electrician)
Repairs to the wall or floor tiles

blocks.p: An objective must be clear enough to plan from and to check at the end. A common test is **SMART**: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound.

head: Too loose to plan from
Clear enough to plan from
rows: Put up a nice canopy for the clinic soon
Fit a 6 m × 3 m painted steel canopy to drawing C-01 rev B, accepted by the client, by 20 March
Make and fit 40 galvanised window grilles to drawing G-02 rev A, with no snags open at handover, within 16 working days of the deposit

head: Source
What it tells you
What to check
rows: Latest revision? All sheets? Sizes add up?
Materials, finish, tests, standards to meet
Does it agree with the drawing?
Standard or code (such as the AWS code the Centre uses)
Rules for welds, welders and inspection
Does it cover these joints, positions and thicknesses?
Dates, working hours, access, site rules, permits, who approves
Real sizes, access, power, ground, hazards, people nearby
Recorded, with photos and a sketch?
How long similar tasks really took, and what went wrong
Is the old job similar enough?

blocks.p: When two documents disagree, for example the sketch shows one post size and the specification another, do not guess and do not simply pick the cheaper or the bigger. Send a **request for information (RFI)**: a formal written question to the client or designer. Record the written answer with the job documents before you plan that part.

ul: Measure and confirm the sizes yourself; check the fixing points and the condition of the walls, floors and concrete.
Access for vehicles, long lengths of steel and any crane; where materials can be stored safely and securely.
Power: is there a 220 V supply that can run a welding machine, or is a generator or an engine-driven welder needed?
Working hours and noise limits; people nearby, such as patients, guests, students or the public.
Overhead lines, ground conditions, drains and anything that can burn.
Site rules and the permits the client uses; the nearest hospital or clinic and the emergency route.

blocks.note: On many rural sites the only supply is a light 110 V or shared domestic circuit that cannot run a welding machine. Find this out at the visit, and plan an engine-driven welder or a generator, with its fuel, transport and a safe place for it to run.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Record the scope, the objectives, the exclusions, the key dates and any assumptions in a **scope statement**. The client and your supervisor sign it before detailed planning goes on. It is the yardstick for every later question about what was agreed.
A **work breakdown structure (WBS)** splits the job into parts, then into tasks small enough to estimate, give to one person or team, and check.

head: Part of the job
Tasks
rows: Site survey; drawings approved; RFIs answered; materials ordered; permits arranged
Cut parts; fit and tack frames; weld frames; make brackets
Fit-up check; weld inspection; size check
Clean; prime; paint (or send to the galvaniser)
Deliver; lift and fix; fit sheeting; touch up paint

ul: Most tasks are **finish-to-start**: one must finish before the next can start (cut before you weld).
Measure on site before you cut anything for it.
Inspect welds **before** painting or galvanising: paint hides faults, and a repair afterwards means stripping and recoating.
Finish all welding before galvanising: welding afterwards burns off the zinc and gives off zinc fume.
A **lag** is a waiting time between tasks with no work in it: primer drying before the topcoat, concrete bases curing before posts are fixed.
Look for tasks that can run **in parallel**, done by different people at the same time: brackets made while the frames are welded, the site prepared while the steel is at the galvaniser.

blocks.p: A **bar chart**, also called a **Gantt chart** after Henry Gantt, who made it popular, lists the tasks down the side and shows each as a bar against a timeline. Milestones are shown as diamonds. The first agreed version is the **baseline**; progress is shaded in as work is done, so delays show at a glance.
A **milestone** is a key point in the job with no work of its own, such as 'materials on site', 'fit-up passed' or 'handover signed'. Milestones give the team and the client clear check points.

The **critical path** is the longest chain of linked tasks through the job. It sets the shortest time in which the whole job can be finished. **Float** (or slack) is how long a task can slip without delaying the finish.

flow: List each task, its duration and the tasks it must wait for
Forward pass: each task starts the day after the latest of the tasks it waits for ends; work out its earliest start and finish
The job length is the latest earliest-finish of all the tasks
Backward pass: from the end, find the latest day each task can finish without delaying the job
Float = latest start − earliest start
Tasks with no float form the critical path

blocks.p: **Worked example: four security doors.** Days are working days, counted from day 1.

head: Task
Days
Waits for
Earliest days
Float
rows: D Make hinge and lock brackets
4 days: it need only finish by day 8
G Prepare the openings on site
9 days: it need only finish by day 11

blocks.p: The critical path is A, B, C, E, F, H: 3 + 2 + 3 + 1 + 2 + 1 = **12 working days**. D could start as late as day 8 and G as late as day 10 without delaying the job.

blocks.note: A one-day slip on a critical task moves the finish one day later, unless you win the time back somewhere else on the critical path. A slip inside a task's float does not move the finish, but it uses up that float, and the task may then become critical.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Float is a tool: it lets you move a non-critical task to free a welder or a machine for a critical one. Watch the critical tasks most closely, every day.

Count working days on a calendar, skipping weekends, public holidays and any days the shop is closed. Example: a job that starts on Thursday 5 November 2026 and needs 6 working days (Monday to Friday) runs Thursday 5, Friday 6, Monday 9, Tuesday 10, Wednesday 11 and Thursday 12, so it finishes on **Thursday 12 November**.
Each task needs people with the right skills, the right equipment and the right materials, all at the right time. The plan shows what is needed, when, and how you will make sure it is there.

ul: Work out the hours each task needs and who can do it. Days needed = total hours ÷ (number of people × hours each works a day). For example, 90 welder-hours with 2 welders on 7.5-hour days takes 90 ÷ 15 = **6 working days**.
Check who is free on each day, allowing for leave, training and other jobs.

Name the **qualified people** where the work needs them: welders qualified to the WPS for coded work such as pressure pipe or structural steel to a code; a trained crane operator and slinger or signaller for lifts; first aiders.
Avoid peaks: two welders on Monday, four on Tuesday and one on Wednesday wastes people. Use float to move non-critical tasks and **level** the labour.
List the machines, tools, lifting gear, access equipment (scaffold, mobile platform) and generators each task needs.
Book them for the right days: another job may need the same machine. Hired items often have a minimum hire period, so a one-day lift may be charged as two.
Check that equipment is serviced and that lifting gear has a current inspection record.
Plan a backup method for key machines: if the plasma cutter fails, the saw or the oxy-fuel set takes over.

flow: Make the cut list from the drawing: every part, its section, length and quantity
Group the parts by section size
Nest the parts into stock lengths or sheets, and add a waste allowance
Make the order list, and check each item's lead time with the supplier
Put the delivery dates in the schedule
On arrival, check sizes, grade, quantity, damage and certificates against the order
Store steel off the ground, covered, and stainless steel apart from carbon steel

blocks.p: **Nesting** means working out how the pieces fit into the stock lengths. Dividing the total metres by the stock length can under-order, because the offcuts may be too short to use.

head: Example
Working
Order
rows: 30 posts of 1.4 m from 6 m tube
Each 6 m length gives 4 posts (5.6 m) and a 0.4 m offcut; 30 ÷ 4 = 7.5
8 lengths (total metres alone, 42 m ÷ 6, would suggest only 7)
58 m of top rail, 6 m lengths, 10% waste
Brackets 380 × 290 mm from a 2.4 m × 1.2 m sheet; 70 needed
6 fit along the 2.4 m side (2280 mm) and 4 across the 1.2 m side (1160 mm), leaving room for the cut width: 24 per sheet; 70 ÷ 24 = 2.9
3 sheets (check the cut width: parts that divide a sheet exactly will not all fit)

blocks.p: The **lead time** is the time from ordering an item to it arriving. Common sizes may come in a day or two; stainless steel, special sections, large plate and fittings can take weeks. Outside work has its own lead time too, such as the galvaniser's turnaround. Set the start date only when you know the materials will be there.

blocks.note: Much steel and most special items are imported, so a missed ship can add weeks. In the hurricane season (1 June to 30 November) shipping and deliveries can be disrupted. Confirm stock with the supplier before you promise dates, and name a second supplier for key items.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: An **estimate** is your best forecast of the time and the cost. Build it from the task list, not from a guess at the whole job.

flow: Hours for each task, from records of similar jobs
Labour cost: hours × the labour rate
Materials from the cut list and fittings list, with waste, priced from current supplier quotes
Outside work (galvanising, blasting), equipment hire, consumables (gas, wire, electrodes, discs) and transport
Add these to get the direct cost
Add overheads and profit as the company's rules say
Add a contingency for the risks
GCT at the current rate, on its own line

head: Worked example: canopy job
Working
J$
rows: Total before overheads, profit and GCT

blocks.p: A **contingency** is an allowance of time or money for risks that may happen: rain, late delivery, a price rise, re-work. It is not hidden profit. Size it from the risks (often somewhere between 5% and 15% of the direct cost, by the company's rules and the job's risks), say what it is for, and agree who may use it.
Show GCT on a separate line, 'at the current rate'. The Government sets the rate and can change it, and the client must see the price before and after tax. Never build an old rate into your figures.

Write down what the estimate assumes: for example, the client provides a clear site and power, work is Monday to Friday 7 a.m. to 4 p.m., and the post holes need no rock breaking. If an assumption turns out wrong, the estimate can be checked and changed fairly.

blocks.note: Check an estimate a second way before it goes out. For example, compare the total with a similar past job, or check that the labour is a sensible share of the cost. A figure ten times too big or too small is usually a slip with a decimal point.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Planning for safety, permits and the unexpected

flow: Identify the hazards of each task and of the site
Decide who could be harmed: the team, the client's staff, the public
Judge how likely harm is and how serious it would be
Choose controls, starting at the top of the hierarchy
Record the assessment, brief the team, and check it while the work goes on

head: Hierarchy of control (most effective first)
Example on a fabrication job
rows: Make and weld the frames in the shop and bolt them in on site, so there is no hot work on site
Cut by saw instead of with a torch near something that can burn
Screens, fume extraction, machine guards, barriers
Permits, safe working times, signs, training, a fire watch
Helmet, gloves, jacket, boots, respirator, harness

blocks.p: A **permit to work** is a written authority from the person in charge of a site, for a particular high-risk task, at a set place and time, with the controls written on it. The plan lists every permit the job needs and who issues it.

head: Permit
When it is needed
Main controls
rows: Welding, cutting or grinding on a client's site, or outside the shop's own set welding areas
Anything that can burn cleared or covered (many permits say within about 10 m)
Extinguisher at hand; gas lines isolated where needed; smoke detectors handled as the site agrees
Fire watch during the work and for the time the permit says afterwards (often 30–60 minutes)
Work inside a tank, vessel, pit or duct
Ventilation; gas testing before entry and while working
Standby person outside; rescue plan and equipment; gas cylinders and machines kept outside
Crane or hoist lifts, especially over people or public places
Load mass checked against the crane's capacity at its radius
Area below closed off with barriers; wind limits
Scaffold or mobile platform; edge protection or harness
Tools tied off; area below closed

blocks.note: In a confined space you cannot see or smell many of the dangers. Shielding gases such as argon and carbon dioxide are heavier than air and collect in low places, pushing out the oxygen; welding fume builds up quickly. Never use oxygen to 'freshen' the air: it makes clothing burn fiercely. Test the air, ventilate, and keep a standby person outside.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: **Galvanised steel:** grind the zinc off the weld area and use fume extraction; zinc fume causes metal fume fever.
**Painted or coated steel:** remove the coating from the weld area; burning paint gives off harmful fumes.
**Stainless steel:** its fume contains chromium compounds; use extraction and the respirator the risk assessment names.
First aiders and first-aid kit; the nearest hospital or clinic and the route to it.
Emergency numbers in Jamaica: 110 for fire and ambulance, 119 for police.
Fire extinguishers and the assembly point.
How an injured worker will be brought out of a tank or down from height: this needs planning **before** anyone goes in or up.

blocks.p: List what could go wrong, judge how likely and how serious each risk is, and plan a backup for the main ones, with the point at which you switch to it.

head: Risk
Backup plan
rows: Make and paint as much as possible in the shop; plan indoor tasks for wet days; shelter and covers ready; no welding in the rain
Order early; confirm stock; name a second supplier
Spare machine, or hire booked in advance; a backup method
A trained, qualified person from another team
Stop lifts and work at height; tie down or remove loose sheets and steel; secure the site

blocks.note: Plan site work around the weather: the wettest months are often May to June and September to November, and the hurricane season runs from 1 June to 30 November. Keep spare time in the schedule for wet days.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Planning for quality: the inspection and test plan

blocks.p: Quality is planned in from the start; it cannot be inspected in at the end. An **inspection and test plan (ITP)** lists every check on the job, in the order of the work: what is checked, how, what it must meet (the **acceptance criteria**), who checks it, and the record that proves it.

head: Stage
Check
Who
Point
Record
rows: Latest revision issued to the shop
Qualified for the WPS where the job needs it
Sizes and holes against the drawing
Visual inspection: size, profile, surface faults; other tests the specification asks for
Surface cleanliness; paint or zinc thickness
Everything against the drawing and specification

head: Term
What it means for the team
rows: Work **stops** at this stage until the named person has checked it and signed it off
The client or their inspector is told in advance and may come to watch; if they were properly notified and do not come, the work may go on, and the record says so
The first item of a batch is checked before the rest are made, so a set-up mistake is caught once, not repeated many times
The measurable standard an item must meet, such as a size tolerance or the weld faults the code allows

blocks.p: The plan names the standard, the drawing and the **revision** the job is built to, so everyone works to the same requirements. Drawings change; an old revision on the shop floor leads to work that has to be redone.

blocks.note: Keep weld inspection ahead of painting and galvanising in the sequence, and make it a hold point. A fault found under paint costs far more to put right than one found on bare steel.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Approving, communicating and running the plan

blocks.p: The plan is approved before work starts: by your **supervisor**, who answers for cost, safety and quality, and by the **client** for anything that touches the scope, the dates, the price or access to their premises. Site permits come from the person in charge of the site.

head: Audience
What they need from the plan
How to present it
rows: The whole plan: scope, schedule, resources, estimate, risk assessment, permits, ITP
Go through it section by section and ask for approval or changes
What will and will not be done, the dates, the price, disruption on site, what the client must provide (power, clear access)
Plain words, the drawing and a simple timeline; written agreement
Their tasks, the order of work, the hazards and controls, permits, hold points, and whom to call
A pre-start briefing; check understanding with questions; give out job sheets

blocks.p: On the first day, brief the whole team: the plan, who does what, the hazards and controls, the permits, the hold points and the emergency arrangements. Ask questions to check that people understood, rather than asking 'Any questions?'. Give a **contacts list**: who to call about materials, safety, design questions and the client, so problems go to the person who can decide.

ul: Walk the job every day: count what is finished and ask the team.
Keep a dated **site diary** or log: work done, people on site, deliveries, weather, problems, instructions received, photos.
Mark progress on the bar chart against the baseline, and compare hours and materials used with the plan.
Look ahead a few days for problems: deliveries, permits, inspections, the weather.
Report progress, delays and the forecast finish to your supervisor each week, or sooner if something goes wrong.

head: Progress check example
Working
rows: A 12-day job planned at an even rate, now at the end of day 6
30% − 50%: the job is 20% behind plan, 12 brackets short

ul: **Delay on a critical task:** act at once. Options include moving people from a task with float, overtime, a second machine, or re-sequencing; weigh the cost against the delay, and tell your supervisor and the client.
**Breakdown:** report it, switch to the backup method, and update the plan. Do not hide it, and do not stop the whole job if other work can go on.

**Change requested by the client:** do not start it straight away. Write down exactly what is wanted, work out the effect on cost, time, materials, safety and work already done, and put it to the supervisor and client as a **variation (change) order**. Go ahead only when it is agreed in writing, then update the drawings, cut list, schedule and the team's job sheets. Even a small change is written down, so nobody argues later about what was asked for or what it cost.

flow: Final inspection against the drawing, the specification and the ITP
Make a snag list of everything still to put right, and clear it
Clean the site; remove waste, offcuts, equipment and barriers
Walk round with the client: show that the work meets what was agreed
Hand over the records and care advice, and get the handover signed
Update the drawings to as-built wherever the work differs
File the plan, changes, records and costs
Hold a review and record the lessons

blocks.p: A **snag list** is a list of small faults or unfinished items that must be put right before handover. An **as-built drawing** has been updated to show the work exactly as it was built, including agreed changes, so that anyone who maintains or alters it later has the true picture.

ul: Drawings, updated to as-built, and the specification
Inspection and test records, material certificates and welder qualification records
Variations, RFIs and their answers, and non-conformance reports
The site diary, the handover sign-off and the final costs

blocks.p: Compare what was planned with what happened, find the causes of the differences, and write down the lessons so the next plan is more accurate and safer.

blocks.note: Work out a percentage difference from the **planned** figure: (actual − planned) ÷ planned × 100. Keep the review about causes, not blame: if welding ran 25% over because fit-up gaps were too wide, the lesson is a better fit-up check and a better estimate next time.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say 'I can' to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can agree and write down a job's scope, including what is not included.
I can write an objective clear enough to plan from and to check at the end.
I can gather and check drawings, specifications, standards and the WPS, and raise an RFI when they disagree.
I can plan and carry out a site visit for a fabrication job.
I can break a job into tasks and put them in a sensible order, with lags and parallel tasks.
I can draw a bar chart, find the critical path, the job length and the float, and mark milestones.
I can turn working days into calendar dates.
I can work out labour days, cut lists, stock lengths, sheets and lead times.
I can level labour and plan equipment, with backups for key machines.
I can build a cost estimate with labour, materials, outside work, equipment, contingency and GCT at the current rate.
I can carry out a risk assessment and name the permits and emergency arrangements a job needs.
I can plan backups for rain, late materials, breakdowns, sickness and storms.
I can write an inspection and test plan with hold points, witness points and records.
I can present a plan to a supervisor, a client and a team, and run a pre-start briefing.
I can track progress, work out how far ahead or behind a job is, and act on delays.
I can handle a change through a written variation order.
I can close out a job and lead a review that improves the next plan.

terms: Acceptance criteria
The measurable standard an item must meet to pass
As-built drawing
A drawing updated to show the work exactly as it was built
Bar chart (Gantt chart)
A chart showing each task as a bar against a timeline
Baseline
The first agreed version of the schedule, which progress is measured against
Contingency
An allowance of time or money for risks that may happen
Critical path
The longest chain of linked tasks; it sets the shortest time to finish the job
Exclusions
Things the scope states are not part of the job
First-off inspection
Checking the first item of a batch before the rest are made
Float (slack)
How long a task can slip without delaying the finish of the job
Hold point
A stage where work stops until a check is signed off
Inspection and test plan (ITP)
A list of every check on a job: what, how, criteria, who, when and the record
Lag
A waiting time between two tasks, such as paint drying
Lead time
The time between ordering an item and it arriving
Milestone
A key point in a job, with no work of its own, used as a check point
Nesting
Fitting the parts on a cut list into stock lengths or sheets with the least waste
Permit to work
Written authority for a high-risk task at a set place and time, with its controls
Request for information (RFI)
A formal written question to the client or designer when information is unclear or conflicting
Resource levelling
Moving tasks within their float to even out the need for people or machines
Scope
What will and will not be done on the job
Site diary
A dated daily record of work, people, deliveries, weather and problems
Snag list
A list of small faults to put right before handover
Variation (change) order
A written, agreed change to the scope, cost or time
Witness point
A stage the client is told about in advance and may come to watch
Work breakdown structure (WBS)
The job split into parts and tasks small enough to plan

c1.title: A canopy for a health centre in Lucea
c1.text: Sheldon Morgan, a Level 3 welder, is planning a steel canopy, about 6 m by 3 m on four posts, over the entrance of a health centre in Lucea, Hanover. The administrator, Mrs Bailey, has sent a sketch that shows 75 × 75 mm posts, and a one-page specification that calls for 100 × 100 mm posts. The canopy must be up before the centre's open day. The posts will stand on concrete bases, but nobody has said who will build them. Patients wait in the entrance area from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m.

c2.title: Market stall frames for Savanna-la-Mar
c2.text: Tamara is planning 20 steel market-stall frames for the market in Savanna-la-Mar, Westmoreland. Her tasks, in working days, are: A order and receive steel, 4; B cut parts, 2, after A; C weld frames, 5, after B; D make canopy brackets, 2, after B; E galvanise, 4, after C and D; F prepare the stall bases at the market, 3, at any time before G; G fix the stalls, 2, after E and F.

c3.title: Handrails for a sports ground near Clark's Town
c3.text: Kirk is planning handrails for the stands at a community sports ground near Clark's Town, Trelawny. The cut list includes 30 posts, each 1.25 m long, cut from 50 mm round tube that comes in 6 m lengths. He expects 72 welder-hours of work, costed at J$1 700 an hour, and the direct cost of the whole job comes to J$420 000. The shop adds a 10% contingency to direct costs.

c4.title: A shutdown at a juice factory near Bog Walk
c4.text: A juice factory near Bog Walk, St Catherine, will shut for three days. Romario's team must TIG weld new brackets, using argon, inside a large stainless steel mixing tank that has been emptied and washed, and replace a galvanised walkway 4 m above the outdoor loading bay. The factory's engineer, Mr Facey, runs the site's permit system. Heavy rain is forecast for two of the three days.

c5.title: Window grilles for a school in Port Maria
c5.text: Sheldon's team is making and fitting 40 window grilles for a primary school in Port Maria, St Mary, in 16 working days, planned at an even rate; grille making is on the critical path. At the end of day 8 he counts 14 grilles finished. On day 10, the school's bursar, Ms Ellis, asks for 6 more grilles for the staff room, and the shop's supervisor agrees the price and time with her on a signed variation order.

questions.q: What should Sheldon do about the two different post sizes?
o: Use the 100 mm posts, because the larger size is always the safer choice
Use 75 mm posts, since the sketch is the newer of the two documents
Send a written request for information and plan that part once answered
Ask the welders which size they would prefer to work with on this job
questions.why: When documents disagree, the planner asks the client or designer in writing (an RFI) and records the answer. Choosing the bigger size can still be wrong: it changes the cost, the base plates and the fixings, and it may not be what the designer intended.

questions.q: Nobody has said who will build the concrete bases. How should Sheldon deal with this in the plan?
o: Leave it out, as builders usually do the bases on jobs like this one
Settle in writing whether the bases are in or out of the shop's scope
Build the bases anyway and add their cost to the final bill at the end
Start making the steel and sort out the bases when the team is on site
questions.why: Anything not clearly excluded is likely to be assumed included. Agreeing in writing who builds the bases, and when they will be ready to take the posts, protects the schedule and the price.

questions.q: Why should the plan take account of the patients waiting in the entrance area?
o: So the team can plan noisy work, sparks and barriers around them
So the team knows how many people will see the finished canopy
Because patients must sign the scope statement before work starts
Because the clinic will pay more if work is done while people wait
questions.why: People near the work can be harmed by arc light, sparks, fumes, noise and lifting. The plan sets working times, screens, barriers and a safe route for patients, agreed with the centre.

questions.q: What is the shortest time in which Tamara's job can be finished?
o: 22 working days
17 working days
20 working days
14 working days
questions.why: The longest chain is A, B, C, E, G: 4 + 2 + 5 + 4 + 2 = 17 days. D and F run alongside other tasks. Adding every task gives 22, which ignores the work done in parallel.

questions.q: Which tasks are on the critical path?
o: A, B, D, E and G
A, B, C, E, F and G
A, B, C, E and G
Only F and G, the site tasks
questions.why: C (5 days) is longer than D (2 days), so the path through C sets the finish. F can be done at any time before G, so it is not on the critical path.

questions.q: How much float does task D (the canopy brackets) have?
o: 2 days
5 days
No float
3 days
questions.why: B ends on day 6. D can start on day 7, but E waits for C, which ends on day 11. D only has to finish by day 11, so it can start as late as day 10: 10 − 7 = 3 days of float.

questions.q: Tamara wants the base-preparation team to finish another job first. What is the latest day task F can start without delaying the whole job?
o: Day 1
Day 13
Day 16
Day 10
questions.why: G starts on day 16, after E finishes on day 15. F (3 days) must be finished by the end of day 15, so it can start as late as day 13. Starting on day 16 would delay G.

questions.q: How many 6 m lengths of tube should Kirk order for the 30 posts?
o: 6 lengths
7 lengths
8 lengths
10 lengths
questions.why: Each 6 m length gives four 1.25 m posts (5 m) with a 1 m offcut, so 30 posts need 30 ÷ 4 = 7.5, rounded up to 8 lengths. Total metres alone (37.5 m ÷ 6) would suggest 7, which leaves the shop two posts short.

questions.q: What is the labour cost for the 72 welder-hours?
questions.why: 72 hours × J$1 700 = J$122 400. The 72 hours are already the total for all the welders, so doubling for two welders (J$244 800) counts the work twice.

questions.q: What is the total of Kirk's direct cost and contingency, before overheads, profit and GCT?
questions.why: 10% of J$420 000 is J$42 000, and J$420 000 + J$42 000 = J$462 000. Contingency is added, never taken away, and J$424 200 adds only 1%.

questions.q: Why does welding with argon make the work inside the tank more dangerous?
o: Argon catches fire easily if a spark reaches it anywhere inside the tank
Argon reacts with juice left in the tank to give off an acid gas
Argon makes the fume from stainless steel far more poisonous
Argon is heavier than air and can collect and push out the oxygen
questions.why: Argon does not burn and cannot be seen or smelt, but it sinks and builds up in a tank, so a welder can collapse from lack of oxygen. The plan needs ventilation, air testing before and during the work, and a standby person outside.

questions.q: Which way of doing the walkway work removes the most hot-work risk on site?
o: Weld it in place at night, when the factory is quiet and empty
Make and weld the sections in the shop, then bolt them in on site
Weld it in place, with harnesses on and a fire extinguisher close by
Weld it in place, but finish faster by using two welders at once
questions.why: Eliminating hot work on site is the most effective control: there is nothing to set alight and less welding at height. Extinguishers and harnesses are still needed for what remains, but they come lower in the hierarchy.

questions.q: With rain forecast for two of the three days, how should Romario order the work?
o: Do the tank work on the wet days and keep the walkway for the dry day
Do the walkway first, as rain on steel does not stop welding outside
Ask the factory for a fourth shutdown day straight away, before any rain
Do both jobs at the same time to finish before the rain gets heavy
questions.why: The tank work is indoors, so it can go on in the rain; outdoor welding at height cannot. Re-sequencing tasks uses the weather instead of fighting it.

questions.q: Which emergency arrangement must be planned specially for the work in the tank?
o: The phone number of the factory's own security guard on the gate
A list of the nearest hardware stores that sell spare welding parts
A rescue plan, with equipment, to get a welder out if he collapses
A first-aid box placed in the factory office for the whole three days
questions.why: A collapsed worker in a tank cannot be reached quickly without a planned rescue method and equipment. Untrained rescuers who go in often become victims too, so the rescue is planned before anyone enters.

questions.q: At the end of day 8, how does the grille work stand against the plan?
o: About 15% ahead of the plan, as 14 grilles are more than a third
About 15% behind the plan: 6 grilles short of the 20 planned
On the plan, because half of the working days are still left
About 35% behind the plan, as only 14 grilles are finished
questions.why: At an even rate, day 8 of 16 should show 50%, which is 20 grilles. 14 of 40 is 35%, so the job is 15% behind, 6 grilles short. Because grille making is critical, the finish date is at risk.

questions.q: Which action best recovers the lost time on the grilles?
o: Skip the fit-up checks for a few days to save some welding time
Wait for the team to speed up as it gets used to the work
Say nothing to the school and hope to finish on the day
Add a welder from a task with float, after checking the cost
questions.why: Moving people from a task that has float to the critical task wins time back without delaying anything else. Skipping checks only moves the problem to handover, and waiting rarely recovers lost time.

questions.q: The variation for 6 more grilles is signed. What must Sheldon update next?
o: Only the final invoice, which is the one place the extra cost appears
Only the bar chart, as the price and the drawings stay the same
The drawings, cut list, order, bar chart and the team's job sheets
Nothing until handover, when all the changes are written up at once
questions.why: A signed variation changes the work itself, so every document the team works from must change with it, and the team must be told. Otherwise the extra grilles are not cut, ordered or scheduled.

questions.q: At the review, the grilles took 104 welding hours against 80 planned. By what percentage was the estimate exceeded?
o: About 23%
questions.why: The overrun is 104 − 80 = 24 hours, and 24 ÷ 80 × 100 = 30%. The percentage is worked from the planned figure; dividing by the actual 104 gives the wrong answer of about 23%.

questions.q: An ITP marks the weld inspection of a frame as a witness point. The client's inspector was told the time in writing but does not arrive. What may the team do?
o: Stop all work on the frame until the inspector comes, however long
Go on with the inspection, recording that the inspector was notified
Paint the frame at once so that the job does not fall behind schedule
Ask the welder who made the frame to sign the inspection as passed
questions.why: At a witness point the client may attend but the work does not wait if they were properly notified; the record shows the notice was given. Work must stop and wait only at a hold point.

questions.q: A plan says the first of 60 brackets must be measured and signed off before the rest are cut and drilled. Why?
o: So that a set-up mistake is caught before 59 more are made wrong
So that the first bracket can be kept as a spare in case of damage
So that the client can see a sample bracket before paying for them
So that the welder can rest while the first bracket is being checked
questions.why: A first-off check catches a wrong stop, template or hole position once, at the cost of one bracket, instead of on the whole batch.
